title: SimpliHuMoN: Simplifying Human Motion Prediction
claim: A single unified transformer maps past poses and trajectories plus learnable queries to multiple future motion proposals, without task-specific modules.
layout: 3 sections, left-to-right, dashed color-coded branches for trajectory vs pose
description: A wide left-to-right block diagram split into three labeled sections (2.1, 2.2, 2.3). On the left, a sketch of past skeleton poses and trajectory curves feeds two dashed branches. A blue branch carries the trajectory T_past through a linear layer, and a green branch carries the pose P_past through an MLP. Learnable queries Q_in go through a linear layer and split into Q_T and Q_P. Each branch passes through a tilde (noise/embedding) circle and a plus circle that adds a shared type embedding E, then concatenation circles (C) produce the context C and the queries Q. These enter a pink transformer block (×L) containing MHSA and FFN. The output Z goes through a purple linear layer into K colored proposal stacks. Each proposal is decoded by a linear head and an MLP head, and the two are summed into X_fut^k. Small skeleton and trajectory plots sit at the output.
caption: An overview of our architecture. Past observations of 3D poses (Ppast) and trajectories (Tpast) are jointly processed by an encoder. abstract: Human motion prediction combines the tasks of trajectory forecasting and human pose prediction. For each of the two tasks, specialized models have been developed. Combining these models for holistic human motion prediction is non-trivial, and recent methods have struggled to compete on established benchmarks for individual tasks. To address this, we propose a simple yet effective transformer-based model for human motion prediction. The model employs a stack of self-attention modules to effectively capture both spatial dependencies within a pose and temporal relationships across a motion sequence. This simple, streamlined, end-to-end model is sufficiently versatile to handle pose-only, trajectory-only, and combined prediction tasks without task-specific modifications. We demonstrate that this approach achieves state-of-the-art results across all tasks through extensive experiments on a wide range of benchmark datasets, including Human3.6M, AMASS, ETH-UCY, and 3DPW.
